---
title: "Field guide: models, infrastructure and evaluation"
description: "How models are produced, served, compared and audited"
---

Some terms describe how a model was produced; others describe how it is served or evaluated. Keeping these stages separate prevents us from attributing every observed difference to “the model.”

:::

## Weights and parameters {#weights-parameters}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Model background</span>

**In plain English.** Parameters are numerical values adjusted during training. The complete collection of learned parameter values is often called the model's weights.

```python
illustrative_layer = {"weight_1": 0.42, "weight_2": -0.17, "bias": 0.03}
print(len(illustrative_layer))
```

<div class="glossary-output">3</div>

**Why it matters.** The dictionary is only an illustration. Real language models contain very large arrays of learned values, not human-readable facts or rules.

## Pretraining {#pretraining}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Model background</span>

**In plain English.** Pretraining adjusts model weights using a large collection of data before the model is adapted to follow the instructions students normally give it.

```python
training_stage = {
    "name": "pretraining",
    "example_objective": "predict a missing or next token",
    "changes_weights": True,
}
print(training_stage["name"])
```

<div class="glossary-output">pretraining</div>

**Why it matters.** Training data and objectives shape what a model can reproduce, associate and systematically miss.

## Post-training and instruction tuning {#posttraining-instruction-tuning}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Model background</span>

**In plain English.** Post-training is further training after pretraining. Instruction tuning is a form of post-training using examples of instructions and preferred responses to make a model more useful in interaction.

```python
model_history = ["pretraining", "instruction_tuning", "deployment"]
print(model_history[1])
```

<div class="glossary-output">instruction_tuning</div>

**Common confusion.** A helpful chat style is not produced by pretraining alone, and post-training does not erase everything learned earlier.

## Fine-tuning and preference optimization {#fine-tuning-preference}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Model background</span>

**In plain English.** Fine-tuning continues training for a more specific objective or dataset. Preference optimization uses comparisons or feedback about outputs to shift model behavior. RLHF is one influential family of such approaches.

```python
training_run = {
    "base_model": "example-base-model",
    "method": "supervised fine-tuning",
    "training_examples": 1200,
}
print(training_run["method"])
```

<div class="glossary-output">supervised fine-tuning</div>

**Why it matters.** “Same architecture” does not mean same behavior when data and post-training differ.

## Distillation {#distillation}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Local models</span>

**In plain English.** Distillation trains a smaller model to reproduce selected behavior of a larger teacher model.

```python
distillation_record = {
    "teacher": "larger-model",
    "student": "smaller-model",
    "target": "teacher-generated responses",
}
print(distillation_record["teacher"], "→", distillation_record["student"])
```

<div class="glossary-output">larger-model → smaller-model</div>

**Why it matters.** A distilled model can be cheaper or easier to run locally but may reproduce only part of the teacher's behavior.

## Quantization {#quantization}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Local models</span>

**In plain English.** Quantization stores or computes model values at reduced numerical precision to lower memory and compute requirements.

```python
model_artifacts = {
    "full_precision_gb": 16.0,
    "quantized_gb": 4.3,
}
saved_gb = model_artifacts["full_precision_gb"] - model_artifacts["quantized_gb"]
print(saved_gb)
```

<div class="glossary-output">11.7</div>

**Why it matters.** Quantization can make local inference feasible, but the exact artifact and quantization method become part of the reproducibility record.

## Mixture of experts {#mixture-of-experts}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Model background</span>

**In plain English.** A mixture-of-experts model contains multiple parameter groups and a routing mechanism that activates a subset for a particular token or input.

```python
experts = ["expert_A", "expert_B", "expert_C", "expert_D"]
activated = experts[1:3]
print(activated)
```

<div class="glossary-output">['expert_B', 'expert_C']</div>

**Common confusion.** The Python slice illustrates selecting a subset; it is not the learned routing computation used inside a real model.

## Provider and routing {#provider-routing}

<span class="term-meta">Useful · Weeks 1, 8 and 13</span>

**In plain English.** A provider operates the infrastructure that serves a model. Routing selects which provider or endpoint handles a request.

```python
run = {
    "requested_model": "openai/gpt-5.2",
    "route": "openrouter",
    "provider": "provider reported in response",
}
print(run["route"], "→", run["provider"])
```

<div class="glossary-output">openrouter → provider reported in response</div>

**Why it matters.** A request may keep the same model slug while its serving route changes. Record provider information when the API exposes it.

## Batching, rate limits and latency {#serving-constraints}

<span class="term-meta">Useful · Weeks 8–13</span>

**In plain English.** Batching groups work for efficient processing. A rate limit restricts requests or tokens over time. Latency is the elapsed time before a result returns.

```python
serving_record = {
    "cases_in_batch": 5,
    "requests_per_minute_limit": 20,
    "latency_seconds": 1.4,
}
print(serving_record)
```

<div class="glossary-output">{'cases_in_batch': 5, 'requests_per_minute_limit': 20, 'latency_seconds': 1.4}</div>

**Why it matters.** Serving constraints affect study cost, missing returns and whether cases were processed under comparable conditions.

## Benchmark and evaluation {#benchmark-evaluation}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Weeks 2–13</span>

**In plain English.** An evaluation measures performance under specified tasks and criteria. A benchmark is a reusable task, dataset or suite used for comparison.

```python
reference_labels = ["SUPPORT", "OPPOSE", "UNCLEAR"]
model_labels = ["SUPPORT", "SUPPORT", "UNCLEAR"]
matches = [reference == model for reference, model in zip(reference_labels, model_labels)]
accuracy = sum(matches) / len(matches)
print(round(accuracy, 2))
```

<div class="glossary-output">0.67</div>

**Why it matters.** A benchmark result applies to that dataset, task formulation, metric and execution setup. It is not a context-free measure of intelligence.

## Calibration {#calibration}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Weeks 7–8</span>

**In plain English.** Calibration asks whether stated probabilities correspond to observed frequencies across comparable predictions.

```python
predicted_probabilities = [0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8]
observed_outcomes = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0]
print("Mean prediction:", sum(predicted_probabilities) / len(predicted_probabilities))
print("Observed rate:", sum(observed_outcomes) / len(observed_outcomes))
```

<div class="glossary-output">Mean prediction: 0.8
Observed rate: 0.6</div>

**Why it matters.** One set this small cannot establish calibration, but it shows what must be compared. Confident prose is not a probability estimate.

## Reliability, prompt sensitivity and reproducibility {#reliability-reproducibility}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Weeks 1–2 and 12</span>

**In plain English.** Reliability concerns consistency under a defined repetition or variation. Prompt sensitivity is change associated with changes in wording or prompt construction. Reproducibility asks whether a recorded procedure can be rerun and whether resulting differences can be explained.

```python
outputs = ["SUPPORT", "SUPPORT", "UNCLEAR", "SUPPORT"]
support_rate = outputs.count("SUPPORT") / len(outputs)
print(support_rate)
```

<div class="glossary-output">0.75</div>

**Why it matters.** The calculation summarizes agreement across four returns. A real audit must state what changed across runs and what was held fixed.

## Hallucination and grounding {#hallucination-grounding}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Weeks 3 and 11</span>

**In plain English.** Hallucination is commonly used for generated content that is unsupported or false. Grounding links an answer to supplied evidence or an external source that can be inspected.

```python
claim = {"text": "T01 immediately joined the group.", "source_ids": ["T01_A"]}
source = {"T01_A": "At that point I did not know who organized them."}
print(source[claim["source_ids"][0]])
```

<div class="glossary-output">At that point I did not know who organized them.</div>

**Why it matters.** Retrieving the cited passage reveals that the claim is not supported. Grounding requires an actual comparison, not merely a citation-shaped string.

## Model versioning and drift {#model-drift}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Weeks 12–13</span>

**In plain English.** Versioning identifies the model artifact used at a time. Drift is change in observed behavior or service conditions across time.

```python
run_one = {"date": "2026-09-01", "model": "model-v1", "label": "SUPPORT"}
run_two = {"date": "2026-11-01", "model": "model-v2", "label": "UNCLEAR"}
changed_fields = [key for key in run_one if run_one[key] != run_two[key]]
print(changed_fields)
```

<div class="glossary-output">['date', 'model', 'label']</div>

**Why it matters.** The records show several simultaneous changes. They do not, on their own, identify which change caused the different label.
